title: What Keeps a Cell a Stem Cell?

scenes.tts: What keeps a cell in the stem-cell state? Chapter one showed a pool that lasts while its clones come and go. But the crypt base held only a few positions. What limits them? Watch the same crypt, now with its signals drawn in.
scenes.visual: Open on chapter 1's carried world: the same large schematic mouse small-intestinal crypt, filling at least 70% of frame height, with blue cells at its rounded base, a teal bracket labelled 'stem-cell pool', and grey daughters streaming upward and out of the top. Put the gold question beside the crypt on the opening sentence. Then briefly flash the yellow winning clone from chapter 1 across the base and let it settle back to blue. Keep 'simplified schematic' visible at full opacity; the upward stream never stops.
scenes.narration: What keeps a cell in the stem-cell state? Chapter one showed a pool that lasts while its clones come and go. But the crypt base held only a few positions. What limits them? Watch the same crypt, now with its signals drawn in.

scenes.visual: Keep the crypt moving. Briefly place the title 'What Keeps a Cell a Stem Cell?' above it, then shrink it into a small corner label without cutting away.

scenes.tts: Start with the neighbourhood. A stem-cell niche is the local environment around stem cells. Its contact and signals bias whether a daughter keeps a stem-cell position or differentiates. In the mouse gut, Paneth cells in the lining and stromal cells beneath it both contribute.
scenes.visual: Chapter 1's soft 'niche support' glow at the crypt base grows into a labelled zone 'niche'. Granule-filled Paneth cartoons (in the lining, wedged between the blue cells) light up, then a layer of flat stromal cells beneath the crypt wall lights up, each with a short label: 'Paneth cells' and 'stromal cells'. Thin arrows pulse from both toward the blue base cells.
scenes.narration: Start with the neighbourhood. A stem-cell niche is the local environment around stem cells. Its contact and signals bias whether a daughter keeps a stem-cell position or differentiates. In the mouse gut, Paneth cells in the lining and stromal cells beneath it both contribute.

scenes.tts: Two kinds of signal run in opposite directions. Wnt is strongest at the crypt base and promotes self-renewal. R-spondin, E G F and Notch also support the base. B M P is strongest higher up, among differentiated cells, and it suppresses self-renewal.
scenes.caption: Two kinds of signal run in opposite directions. Wnt is strongest at the crypt base and promotes self-renewal. R-spondin, EGF and Notch also support the base. BMP is strongest higher up, among differentiated cells, and it suppresses self-renewal.
scenes.visual: Fill the crypt with two schematic colour gradients that slowly shimmer: warm orange 'Wnt' densest at the base and fading upward; purple 'BMP' densest high in the crypt among the grey cells and fading downward. A small chip 'also: R-spondin, EGF, Notch' attaches to the orange base. Add a vertical bar at the side labelled 'schematic gradient' (not measured). The grey stream keeps rising through both colours.
scenes.narration: Two kinds of signal run in opposite directions. Wnt is strongest at the crypt base and promotes self-renewal. R-spondin, EGF and Notch also support the base. BMP is strongest higher up, among differentiated cells, and it suppresses self-renewal.

scenes.tts: During cell turnover, a blue stem cell is displaced upward, away from the strongest Wnt. What do you expect it to do?
scenes.visual: In the carried crypt, one blue base cell is nudged up into the fading orange and rising purple while a neighbouring blue cell fills its vacated base position. Freeze the displaced cell's position with a gold ring and put the gold question in large text above the crypt.
scenes.narration: During cell turnover, a blue stem cell is displaced upward, away from the strongest Wnt. What do you expect it to do?

scenes.visual: Hold the gold question and the ringed cell. The other cells keep a very slow upward drift and the gradients shimmer gently. No new labels appear.

scenes.tts: As cells move up, they become more likely to leave the stem-cell state. Less Wnt reaches them, and more B M P. The cell that remains at the base keeps its support. So the positions are limited because the support is local.
scenes.caption: As cells move up, they become more likely to leave the stem-cell state. Less Wnt reaches them, and more BMP. The cell that remains at the base keeps its support. So the positions are limited because the support is local.
scenes.visual: The ringed cell drifts upward and its blue fades to grey as purple surrounds it; it turns into a simple epithelial silhouette and joins the rising stream. The neighbouring cell remains blue in the orange zone. Then outline the orange base zone with the teal pool bracket from chapter 1, so the bracket and the high-Wnt zone visibly coincide. Label: 'local support'.
scenes.narration: As cells move up, they become more likely to leave the stem-cell state. Less Wnt reaches them, and more BMP. The cell that remains at the base keeps its support. So the positions are limited because the support is local.

scenes.tts: Here is the key idea. In the mouse gut, being a stem cell looks less fixed. It looks more like a state that local signals support. Chapter one's clones competed for places inside that support. A winner holds a place, not a permanent title.
scenes.visual: Pull back slightly so the whole crypt and gradients are visible. Show a blue cell in the orange zone with a label 'state', and a dashed arrow from the zone to the cell labelled 'supported by niche'. Briefly replay chapter 1's Confetti colours jostling inside the teal bracket, all within the orange zone.
scenes.narration: Here is the key idea. In the mouse gut, being a stem cell looks less fixed. It looks more like a state that local signals support. Chapter one's clones competed for places inside that support. A winner holds a place, not a permanent title.

scenes.tts: A dish tests how much surroundings matter. Single sorted L G R five cells grew into organoids with matrix and added factors. Organoids are crypt-villus structures grown in culture. They could be replated repeatedly. No stromal cells were present; the matrix and factors supplied a niche.
scenes.caption: A dish tests how much surroundings matter. Single sorted Lgr5 cells grew into organoids with matrix and added factors. Organoids are crypt-villus structures grown in culture. They could be replated repeatedly. No stromal cells were present; the matrix and factors supplied a niche.
scenes.visual: Lift one blue cell out of the crypt into a round dish at the side. Add a pale gel labelled 'matrix' and three small droplets labelled 'added factors'. The single cell divides and folds into a budding organoid with small crypt-like buds and a central lumen, labelled 'organoid (schematic)'. Show a crossed-out stromal-cell icon beside the dish, and keep a faint orange glow at each bud base.
scenes.narration: A dish tests how much surroundings matter. Single sorted Lgr5 cells grew into organoids with matrix and added factors. Organoids are crypt-villus structures grown in culture. They could be replated repeatedly. No stromal cells were present; the matrix and factors supplied a niche.

scenes.tts: If the state depends on support, a harder question follows. Could a cell that has already left the base come back? Injury tests that, when the usual stem cells are lost. Reprogramming pushes further, asking whether a specialized nucleus can be reset beyond its tissue.
scenes.visual: Back in the crypt, dim the blue base cells to outlines (no claim about what happens next) and put a gold question mark on one grey cell partway up, with a dashed arrow pointing back down to the base, labelled 'come back?'. Then, to the side, show a small grey specialized cell with its nucleus highlighted and a second, larger gold question mark labelled 'reset beyond the tissue?'. Do not show any outcome.
scenes.narration: If the state depends on support, a harder question follows. Could a cell that has already left the base come back? Injury tests that, when the usual stem cells are lost. Reprogramming pushes further, asking whether a specialized nucleus can be reset beyond its tissue.

scenes.tts: So when you ask who is a stem cell, look at the place as well as the cell. Local niche signals help hold a cell in the stem-cell state. Whether a cell that left can return is the next test.
scenes.visual: Return to the full crypt with its orange and purple gradients, blue base cells inside the teal bracket and the grey stream rising. Brighten the orange base zone as the narrator says 'local niche signals', then dim all labels except the final rule, keeping the crypt moving behind it.
scenes.narration: So when you ask who is a stem cell, look at the place as well as the cell. Local niche signals help hold a cell in the stem-cell state. Whether a cell that left can return is the next test.

scenes.visual: End card over the still-living crypt: 'Local niche signals help hold a cell in the stem-cell state.' Keep the gradients gently shimmering and the grey cells rising until the cut.
